extracted.intended_audience: educational institutions, school administrators, legal counsel, and other stakeholders responsible for Title IX compliance
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretation and application guidance for the Department of Education's final Title IX regulations (especially §106.31(a)(2)) across contexts such as bathrooms/locker rooms, housing, appearance codes, health services, parental rights, and religious objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on policies excluding participation consistent with gender identity (§106.31(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.31(a)(2) prohibits a recipient from adopting a policy or engaging in a practice that prevents a person from participating in an education program or activity consistent with the person's gender identity when that person seeks to participate consistent with their gender identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prohibition applies regardless of whether the person is transgender or cisgender; it bars policies that exclude or treat persons differently in a way that causes more than de minimis harm. Recipients retain discretion to provide sex‑separate facilities consistent with Title IX's nondiscrimination mandate, but cannot adopt policies that categorically prevent participation consistent with gender identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: De minimis harm standard for sex‑separate facilities and activities
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations prohibit separation or different treatment based on sex that causes more than de minimis harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may maintain sex‑separate facilities, but sex-based distinctions are permissible only to the extent they do not subject any person to more than de minimis harm. This standard is applied in contexts such as bathrooms, locker rooms, and appearance codes; courts' decisions are cited to reject speculative or generalized claims of harm from transgender students' presence (e.g., Grimm, Whitaker, Boyertown, Parents for Priv.). See Section IV.B.1 for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients' discretion to protect privacy and safety without excluding transgender students
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients can make and enforce rules that protect all students' safety and privacy without excluding transgender students from accessing sex‑separate facilities consistent with their gender identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies such as codes of conduct, rules prohibiting harassment/assault, and other nondiscriminatory privacy measures are permitted. The Department disagrees that legitimate privacy/safety goals are inconsistent with §106.31(a)(2). Courts have rejected unsubstantiated assertions that a transgender person's presence in single‑sex spaces inherently compromises others' privacy or safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional provision of single‑occupancy or gender‑neutral facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the regulations requires recipients to provide gender‑neutral or single‑occupancy facilities; recipients may offer them voluntarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department may decline to require such facilities because they are not the only means to provide nondiscriminatory access and because imposing such a requirement could have significant cost implications. Recipients may nonetheless offer them to accommodate privacy preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nondiscriminatory steps allowed to ensure privacy and safety in sex‑separate facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.31(a)(2) does not prohibit recipients from taking nondiscriminatory steps to ensure privacy and safety in sex‑separate facilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include general codes of conduct and enforcement against harassment, assault, and other misconduct. Such steps must be nondiscriminatory and cannot be used as a pretext to exclude persons based on gender identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX covers all operations of an educational institution (including health centers)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a recipient is an educational institution, all of its operations are considered covered by Title IX, including health centers, campus housing, campus services, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This means services like campus health centers and nurses' offices are part of the covered education program or activity and subject to Title IX regulations. For non‑educational recipients, Title IX applies only to education program(s) or activity(ies) they operate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations do not set medical standards of care or require provision of specific medical treatments
rubrics_metrics.description: The Title IX regulations do not (and cannot) promote any particular medical treatment, require provision of particular medical procedures, or set any standard of care; they implement nondiscrimination requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance with Title IX does not interfere with providers' exercise of professional medical judgment. Overlap with HHS Section 1557 may exist for some recipients, but HHS rulemaking is outside this rulemaking's scope; agencies will collaborate as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Housing (living facilities) carve‑out under 20 U.S.C. 1686
rubrics_metrics.description: 20 U.S.C. 1686 expressly permits an educational institution to maintain separate living facilities for the different sexes and thus §106.31(a)(2) does not apply to sex‑separate housing placements to the extent permitted by that statutory carve‑out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This carve‑out is limited to living facilities (housing) and does not extend to other sex‑separate contexts such as bathrooms, locker rooms, or showers, which are governed by the general nondiscrimination mandate (20 U.S.C. 1681) and corresponding regulations (e.g., §106.33). Recipients may voluntarily permit transgender students to access housing consistent with their gender identity, but the statute's housing exception is narrow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental rights preserved; §106.6(g) reinforces parental authority for minors
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the final regulations disturbs parental rights; §106.6(g) reinforces the right of a parent to act on behalf of their minor child, including making complaints under the recipient's grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When parents and minor students disagree about addressing sex discrimination, deference to the judgment of a parent, guardian, or authorized legal representative is appropriate. Recipients may disclose information about a minor child to parents who have legal rights to receive disclosures. See §§106.44(j) and 106.6(g) for additional explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients' Title IX obligations are not excused by State or local law (§106.6(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient's obligation to comply with Title IX and the regulations is not obviated or alleviated by any State or local law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declines to opine generally on interactions with specific State laws (fact‑specific); it refers the public to §106.6(b) for the principle that federal obligations remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and limits of 'parental status' and 'in loco parentis' in regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of 'parental status' (including 'in loco parentis') is limited to certain contexts (e.g., §§106.21(c)(2)(i), 106.37(a)(3), 106.40(a), and 106.57(a)(1)) addressing discrimination related to parental status and does not confer parental authority or alter parental rights under §106.6(g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition is to address sex discrimination related to parental status (e.g., treating mothers differently than fathers) and should not be read to authorize school employees to act as parents or affect parental rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious‑institution exemption and process to claim it (§106.12(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections §§106.10 and 106.31(a)(2) do not apply to an educational institution controlled by a religious organization to the extent the provision's application would be inconsistent with the organization's religious tenets; an institution seeking the exemption may have its highest‑ranking official submit a written statement to the Assistant Secretary for Civil Rights identifying conflicting provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Title IX religious exemption applies to institutions or entities 'controlled by a religious organization' and is not a vehicle to address individual students' or employees' exercise of religion. The Department will consider RFRA and consult with OGC and other agencies as appropriate when evaluating claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction with RFRA and First Amendment protections (§106.6(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: These regulations do not require a recipient to restrict rights protected under the First Amendment; the Department must also act in accordance with RFRA and constitutional protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department cannot predict how RFRA will apply in particular fact patterns; individuals may notify the Department of potential RFRA burdens. The Department considers RFRA when evaluating recipient compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance codes (dress/grooming) are subject to Title IX and §106.31(a)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sex‑specific appearance codes, including dress and grooming codes, are subject to Title IX and §106.31(a)(2); sex‑based distinctions in appearance codes are permissible only to the extent they do not cause more than de minimis harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of permissible sex‑based distinctions include protective gear or uniforms for specific physical education or athletic activities. Imposing different restrictions on how boys and girls dress or appear would violate Title IX if the sex‑specific restriction causes more than de minimis harm. The Department rejects 'comparable burdens' as a defense (citing Bostock and Peltier) and recognizes court decisions affirming Title IX coverage of dress codes (e.g., Peltier, Hayden). The Department will not restore a standalone appearance provision but applies existing prohibitions and §106.31(a)(2) to appearance codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Comparable burdens' defense is not a valid defense to sex discrimination under Title IX
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient cannot defend a sex‑specific appearance code by showing it imposes 'comparable burdens' on both sexes; discriminating against both sexes does not eliminate liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department cites Bostock (Title VII) and Peltier to explain that 'discriminating against members of both sexes does not eliminate liability, but doubles it.' Some courts still use a 'comparable burdens' test, but the Department disagrees with that approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to juvenile justice facilities is limited to education programs/activities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Title IX regulations apply to juvenile justice facilities that receive Federal funds, but only to education programs or activities offered by such facilities; §106.31(a)(2) does not apply where different treatment causing more than de minimis harm is otherwise permitted under Title IX (e.g., living facilities under 20 U.S.C. 1686).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department recognizes juvenile justice facilities' obligations (including PREA) to protect populations, but the generalized data and anecdotes cited do not demonstrate that treating youth consistent with gender identity will increase risk of sexual assault in those facilities.
